p1.key: A Lewis acid accepts an electron pair. In B, H<sup>+</sup> accepts the lone pair from NH<sub>3</sub> to form a coordination bond. In C and D the first species are bases or Brønsted acids, and in A water donates H<sup>+</sup>.
Warm aqueous NaOH supplies OH<sup>−</sup>, a strong nucleophile that substitutes for iodine: CH<sub>3</sub>I + OH<sup>−</sup> → CH<sub>3</sub>OH + I<sup>−</sup>. Water reacts far more slowly.
Alkenes decolorize bromine water by addition across the C=C bond; alkanes do not react. Both burn in excess oxygen to give the same products, so ignition does not distinguish them.

The ester CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub>COO(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>4</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> is pentyl butanoate. The acyl part has 4 C (butanoic acid) and the alkyl part has 5 C (pentan-1-ol). An aldehyde cannot form an ester.

NH3 acts as a nucleophile and substitutes for the halogen. With a large excess of ammonia further substitution is unlikely, so the main product is a primary amine. Too little ammonia leads to more substituted products.
p1.flag: amine formation from halogenoalkanes not explicit in 2025 guide

p1.key: Addition would destroy the stable delocalized π system of benzene, so benzene typically undergoes electrophilic substitution (e.g. nitration), which keeps the ring intact.

I: OH<sup>−</sup> replaces Cl (nucleophilic substitution). II: ethanol is oxidized to ethanoic acid. III: the acid reacts with methanol to form an ester (esterification). D describes III as substitution, which is less specific; the markscheme accepts A only.
Bromine adds across the C=C double bond of ethene in an addition reaction, giving 1,2-dibromoethane, C2H4Br2.
CH<sub>3</sub>CCl<sub>3</sub> is saturated, so it can only undergo substitution. Benzene prefers substitution to keep its delocalized ring. Propene (I) has a C=C bond and undergoes addition.

(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CCl is a tertiary halogenoalkane. It forms a relatively stable tertiary carbocation, and the three methyl groups hinder backside attack, so S<sub>N</sub>1 is favoured. The primary halides react by S<sub>N</sub>2, and chlorobenzene hardly reacts.
Ethanoic acid + ethanol → ethyl ethanoate, CH3COOCH2CH3 + H2O. The acid provides CH3CO— and the alcohol provides —OCH2CH3.
Bromine adds across the C=C bond (electrophilic addition), giving 1,2-dibromoethane, CH2BrCH2Br. Addition, not substitution, so no C=C remains.
A nucleophile needs a lone pair to donate to the δ+ carbon. Ethanol, ethylamine and water all have lone pairs on O or N. Ethane has none.

Dehydration removes water. Within one molecule it gives ethene (CH<sub>2</sub>=CH<sub>2</sub>). Between two molecules it gives ethoxyethane (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OC<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>). Ethanal and ethanoic acid are oxidation products.
CN⁻ ions replace water molecules and donate lone pairs to Fe3+ via coordination bonds, so they act as ligands (Lewis bases, not Lewis acids). No proton transfer or change in oxidation state occurs.
An alcohol (methanol) reacts with a carboxylic acid (propanoic acid) to form an ester (methyl propanoate) and water: this is esterification, a condensation reaction.
Concentrated phosphoric (or sulfuric) acid dehydrates ethanol by removing water: C2H5OH → C2H4 + H2O, giving ethene. It is not an oxidizing agent, so no ethanal or ethanoic acid forms.
p1.flag: dehydration of alcohols not explicitly in 2025 syllabus

p1.key: OH<sup>−</sup> is a nucleophile that substitutes for Br in a halogenoalkane, and Br<sup>−</sup> is a good leaving group. NH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>, OCH<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> and OH<sup>−</sup> are poor leaving groups, so A, B and D don't happen.

Methylbenzene contains a benzene ring, whose delocalized π electrons attract electrophiles; it substitutes rather than adds to keep its aromatic stability. Bromobutane undergoes nucleophilic substitution, and cyclohexane free-radical substitution.
The amine replaces NH3: CH3COOH + CH3CH2NH2 → salt, which on heating loses water to form the N-substituted amide CH3CONHCH2CH3 (a condensation reaction).

Ethanol (M<sub>r</sub> 46) is dehydrated by concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> at 170 °C to ethene, an alkene that decolorizes bromine water. Methoxymethane also has M<sub>r</sub> 46 but cannot form an alkene this way.
p1.flag: dehydration of alcohols not explicitly in 2025 syllabus

p1.key: The rate depends on breaking the C–halogen bond. C–I is the longest and weakest (lowest bond enthalpy), so iodide is the best leaving group and 1-iodopropane hydrolyses fastest. C–F is the strongest.

NH<sub>3</sub> donates lone pairs to Cr<sup>3+</sup> (a Lewis base forming coordination bonds), but no protons are transferred. A, B and C all involve H<sup>+</sup> transfer, so they are Brønsted–Lowry reactions too.
p1.flag: duplicate of 2003M paper (identical images and markscheme)

p1.key: Water adds across the C=C double bond of ethene to form ethanol (hydration), so two molecules combine into one with nothing lost: an addition reaction.
p1.flag: duplicate of 2003M paper (identical images and markscheme)

p1.key: Tertiary halogenoalkanes react by S<sub>N</sub>1 via a stable tertiary carbocation, faster than primary ones (S<sub>N</sub>2). The S<sub>N</sub>1 rate depends only on [halogenoalkane]; iodoalkanes react faster than chloroalkanes.
p1.flag: duplicate of 2003M paper (identical images and markscheme)

p1.key: Pentan-2-ol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, loses H<sub>2</sub>O with a C=C forming next to C2: it gives pent-1-ene, CH<sub>2</sub>=CHCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (or pent-2-ene). The other options have the wrong carbon skeleton.
p1.flag: dehydration of alcohols not explicitly in 2025 syllabus; duplicate of 2003M paper (identical images and markscheme)

p1.key: NH<sub>3</sub> donates lone pairs to Cu<sup>2+</sup> (Lewis acid) to form coordination bonds; no proton is transferred. A, C and D all involve H<sup>+</sup> transfer, so they are also Brønsted–Lowry reactions.
HBr adds across the C=C double bond of ethene (electrophilic addition), giving bromoethane, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br.
Benzene burns (combustion), can be hydrogenated to cyclohexane under harsh conditions with a Ni catalyst, and typically undergoes electrophilic substitution, which keeps the stable delocalized ring.

The tertiary halogenoalkane (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CBr reacts by S<sub>N</sub>1, forming a carbocation intermediate. The primary 1-bromopropane reacts by S<sub>N</sub>2 in one step with no ion intermediate.
Br<sub>2</sub> adds across the C=C double bond, forming a single saturated product: an addition reaction.
S<sub>N</sub>1 is fastest for tertiary halogenoalkanes (most stable carbocation). C–Br is weaker than C–Cl, so (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CBr ionizes faster than (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CCl.
An alcohol and a carboxylic acid condense to form an ester and water: ethanol + ethanoic acid → ethyl ethanoate, CH<sub>3</sub>COOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>. B is methyl ethanoate.
The polar C–X bond makes the carbon δ+, so halogenoalkanes are attacked by nucleophiles (e.g. OH<sup>−</sup>) that replace the halogen: nucleophilic substitution.
HBr adds across the C=C double bond of ethene (electrophilic addition), giving a single product, bromoethane CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br. No H<sub>2</sub> is released.
CH<sub>3</sub>COOCH<sub>3</sub> is methyl ethanoate: the "CH<sub>3</sub>COO" part comes from ethanoic acid and the "CH<sub>3</sub>" part from methanol.

(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CBr is a tertiary halogenoalkane; OH⁻ replaces Br⁻ via an S<sub>N</sub>1 mechanism (a stable tertiary carbocation forms; backside attack for S<sub>N</sub>2 is sterically hindered).

S<sub>N</sub>2 is bimolecular (rate = k[RX][OH⁻]), so doubling [OH⁻] doubles its rate; S<sub>N</sub>1 rate = k[RX] only. Tertiary compounds react faster (S<sub>N</sub>1); C–I is weaker than C–Cl so iodides react faster.

Ethene's C=C double bond allows addition reactions (e.g. with H<sub>2</sub>, Br<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>O) and addition polymerization to poly(ethene). Esterification requires an alcohol and a carboxylic acid.

Tertiary halogenoalkanes react faster (S<sub>N</sub>1 via a stable tertiary carbocation), and the C–Br bond is much weaker than C–F, so Br⁻ is the better leaving group. (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CBr reacts fastest.
A nucleophile donates a lone pair. CH<sub>4</sub> has no lone pairs, so it cannot act as a nucleophile; H<sub>2</sub>O, NH<sub>3</sub> and CN⁻ all have lone pairs.

The fastest hydrolysis (giving the halide precipitate) needs a weak C–X bond and an S<sub>N</sub>1 route: tertiary 2-iodo-2-methylpropane. C–I is weaker than C–Br, and tertiary forms a stable carbocation.
A Lewis base donates an electron pair and a Lewis acid accepts it. NH<sub>3</sub> donates its lone pair to Cu²⁺ (II) and to H⁺ (III). Reaction I is a redox reaction, not a Lewis acid–base reaction.

Chloroethane is a primary halogenoalkane, so OH⁻ attacks the carbon in a single concerted, bimolecular step (S<sub>N</sub>2). There is no carbocation intermediate (that is S<sub>N</sub>1, favoured by tertiary halogenoalkanes).
A ligand must donate a lone pair to the metal ion to form a coordination bond. NH3 and Cl− both have lone pairs; CH4 has none. A: I and II only.
BF3 has an incomplete octet on boron and can accept an electron pair (Lewis acid), but it has no H to donate as a proton, so it is not a Brønsted–Lowry acid. D.

Tertiary halogenoalkanes react mainly by S<sub>N</sub>1, via a stable tertiary carbocation. The C–X bond breaks heterolytically (not A), C–I is weaker so iodoalkanes react faster (not B), and primary ones react by the one-step S<sub>N</sub>2 (not C).
Hydrogenation adds H2 across the C=C bonds in unsaturated vegetable oils (Ni catalyst), raising the melting point to give a solid fat such as margarine.
A Lewis acid is an electron-pair acceptor. A Brønsted–Lowry acid donates a proton. A, B and C mix up the two definitions.
Acid-catalysed hydration adds H and OH across the C=C of hex-3-ene. The alkene is symmetrical, so the product is hexan-3-ol, CH3(CH2)2CH(OH)CH2CH3. A.

The C=C adds bromine, so the orange colour disappears (I) and the product is saturated (II). Addition across C1=C2 puts Br on C1 (e.g. 1,2-dibromohexane), not just 2-bromohexane, which would need HBr. A.

Ethane undergoes free-radical substitution with Cl2 to give chloroethane, then OH− replaces Cl by nucleophilic substitution to give ethanol. A's second step would be substitution, not elimination; C and D use the wrong reaction types. B.
I: Br replaced by OH (nucleophilic substitution). II: propan-1-ol oxidized to propanoic acid. III: acid + ethanol → ester + water (condensation / esterification).
Alkenes react mainly by addition across the C=C (e.g. with H2O to form alcohols, or to form addition polymers), not substitution, so C is the incorrect statement.
(CH3)3CBr is tertiary, so it reacts by SN1: the C–Br bond breaks first to give a carbocation intermediate, which is then attacked by OH⁻.
2-iodo-2-methylpropane is a tertiary halogenoalkane. The bulky groups block backside attack and stabilize a carbocation, so it reacts by S<sub>N</sub>1.

Tertiary halogenoalkanes react fastest (via S<sub>N</sub>1, stable carbocation), and C–I is the weakest carbon–halogen bond, making I⁻ the best leaving group. So the tertiary iodide, B, reacts fastest.
Bromoethane is primary, so CN⁻ (a nucleophile) attacks in a one-step bimolecular SN2 reaction. The C–Br bond breaks heterolytically (Br leaves as Br⁻), so C is the incorrect statement.

The model is CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (ethyl butanoate): a 4-carbon acid part (C=O carbon plus 3 C) and an O–C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub> group. It is made from butanoic acid and ethanol.
A Brønsted–Lowry acid is a proton (H⁺) donor; a Lewis acid is an electron-pair acceptor.
Steam adds H and OH across the C=C of but-2-ene (CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>3</sub>), giving butan-2-ol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHOHCH<sub>3</sub>.
Tertiary halogenoalkanes react fastest (S<sub>N</sub>1 via a stable tertiary carbocation), and the C–I bond is the weakest, so iodide is the best leaving group: 2-iodo-2-methylpropane.
Propan-1-ol + butanoic acid (acid catalyst) form the ester propyl butanoate. Esters have fruity smells and are used in perfumes and flavourings.

HCl adds across the C=C of but-2-ene (CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>3</sub>), giving CH<sub>3</sub>CHClCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>. Alkenes undergo addition, not substitution; Cl<sub>2</sub> would give 2,3-dichlorobutane.

C–F is the strongest carbon–halogen bond, so CH<sub>3</sub>F reacts slowest. C–Cl is weaker, and the secondary (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCl can also react partly by S<sub>N</sub>1 through a more stable carbocation, so it is fastest.

In D, the H<sub>2</sub>O ligands donate lone pairs to Cu<sup>2+</sup> (Lewis base → Lewis acid) with no proton transfer, so it is Lewis only. A, B and C all involve H⁺ transfer, so they are also Brønsted–Lowry reactions.

A carboxylic acid and an amine condense, losing H<sub>2</sub>O, to form an amide: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COOH + CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CONHCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O. The ethyl group ends up on the N.
p1.flag: amide formation from monomers only implied by condensation polymers (S2.4)

p1.key: BF<sub>3</sub> has an incomplete octet on B, so it can accept an electron pair (Lewis acid). It has no H to donate as a proton, so it is not a Brønsted–Lowry acid. The other three can all donate H<sup>+</sup>.

CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>3</sub> (but-2-ene) is an alkene. Bromine adds across the C=C bond (electrophilic addition) without light, so it decolourizes bromine water. The ketone, alcohol and alkane do not react in the dark.

Tertiary halogenoalkanes react fastest (S<sub>N</sub>1, via a stable tertiary carbocation). The C–Br bond is weaker than C–Cl, so bromide is the better leaving group. (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CBr therefore reacts most quickly.

The rate of nucleophilic substitution depends on the nucleophile (e.g. OH<sup>−</sup> is better than H<sub>2</sub>O), the halogen (C–I is weaker than C–Cl, so it reacts faster) and the structure (primary/secondary/tertiary, which affects S<sub>N</sub>1 vs S<sub>N</sub>2).

Each NH<sub>3</sub> donates its lone pair to Ag<sup>+</sup>, forming a coordinate bond. This is a Lewis acid–base reaction: Ag<sup>+</sup> accepts the electron pair. NH<sub>3</sub> is the ligand, not Ag<sup>+</sup>.

In B, Cl<sup>−</sup> ligands replace H<sub>2</sub>O ligands, each donating an electron pair to Co<sup>2+</sup> (the Lewis acid). No proton is transferred between acid and base. A, C and D all involve H<sup>+</sup> transfer, so they are Brønsted–Lowry reactions as well.
Step I is nucleophilic substitution by CN<sup>−</sup> (from KCN), which adds one carbon. Step II reduces the nitrile –C≡N to –CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> using H<sub>2</sub> with a Ni catalyst.

Tertiary halogenoalkanes react fastest (S<sub>N</sub>1 via a stable carbocation), and the C–I bond is the weakest carbon–halogen bond, so iodide leaves most easily. 2-iodo-2-methylpropane therefore reacts fastest.

In D, each H<sub>2</sub>O donates a lone pair to Ni<sup>2+</sup>, replacing NH<sub>3</sub> as a ligand. This is Lewis base behaviour with no proton accepted. In A and C water accepts H<sup>+</sup> (a Brønsted–Lowry base), and in B it donates H<sup>+</sup> to O<sup>2−</sup>.

The molecule is 1-chloro-2-methylpropane, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH<sub>2</sub>Cl. The C bonded to Cl is attached to only one other carbon, so it is primary. Primary halogenoalkanes react with OH<sup>−</sup> mainly by S<sub>N</sub>2. Branching elsewhere does not make it tertiary.

But-2-ene is symmetrical, so adding H<sub>2</sub>O across C=C can only give butan-2-ol. But-1-ene can give both butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol. Alcoholic NaOH causes elimination, giving alkenes rather than alcohols.
A Lewis base is an electron-pair donor. A Brønsted–Lowry base is a proton acceptor, so B and C mix up the two definitions, and A is wrong.
Bromine adds across the C=C double bond of propene, one Br on each of the two former double-bond carbons, giving 1,2-dibromopropane, CH3CHBrCH2Br.

Chloroethane is a primary halogenoalkane, so it reacts by SN2 (bimolecular, heterolytic C–Cl fission). Neutral NH3 attacks neutral C2H5Cl, so the transition state [H3N···C···Cl] carries no overall charge, only partial charges.
Cl2 adds across the C=C of CH3CH=CH2, one Cl to each of the two double-bond carbons (C1 and C2), giving CH3CHClCH2Cl, 1,2-dichloropropane.

Tertiary halogenoalkanes react by S<sub>N</sub>1. The rate-determining step is ionization of the halogenoalkane to a carbocation, so rate = k[halogenoalkane]. Changing the nucleophile or its concentration has no effect.

Ethane undergoes free-radical substitution with Cl<sub>2</sub> (UV) to give C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Cl. Chloroethane then undergoes nucleophilic substitution with ammonia to give ethylamine, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>.
In SN1 the slow, rate-determining step is ionization of R–Br to the carbocation (unimolecular), followed by fast attack by OH−. OH− is not in the slow step, so rate = k[R–Br].

A Lewis acid accepts an electron pair. BF<sub>3</sub> and AlCl<sub>3</sub> have incomplete octets and H<sup>+</sup> has an empty orbital. In CCl<sub>4</sub> carbon has a full octet with no empty low-energy orbital, so it cannot accept a pair.

Br<sub>2</sub> adds across C=C (addition, I) to give 1,2-dibromoethane, which is colourless; the orange-brown bromine is decolourised (II). The product has only single bonds, so it is saturated (III).

Rate increases primary < secondary < tertiary (S<sub>N</sub>1 via a stable tertiary carbocation is fastest). For the same structure, C–Br is weaker than C–Cl, so the bromide reacts faster: primary RCl < secondary RCl < (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CCl < (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CBr.

BF<sub>3</sub> has an incomplete octet on boron, so it accepts an electron pair (Lewis acid), but it has no H<sup>+</sup> to donate, so it cannot be a Brønsted–Lowry acid. H<sub>2</sub>O can donate H<sup>+</sup>; NH<sub>3</sub> and PCl<sub>3</sub> are Lewis bases.

Bromine water is decolourised by alkenes (electrophilic addition). Pent-2-ene (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>3</sub>) decolourises it; pentane, a saturated alkane, does not react in the dark. The other pairs are both saturated.

Tertiary halogenoalkanes react fastest (S<sub>N</sub>1 via a stable tertiary carbocation), and the C–Br bond is weaker than C–Cl, so it breaks more easily. So (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CBr is fastest.
In Al2Cl6, a bridging Cl atom donates a lone pair to the electron-deficient Al atom of the other AlCl3 unit, forming coordinate bonds. Both Al atoms accept electron pairs, so both act as Lewis acids.

1-chloropropane is primary, so it reacts by SN2: one concerted step in which OH− acts as a nucleophile (not a Brønsted–Lowry base). Rate = k[RCl][OH−], which is second order. Products are propan-1-ol and Cl−, not water.
Doubling [C4H9Br] doubles the rate; doubling [OH−] has no effect. So rate = k[C4H9Br], a unimolecular rate-determining step: SN1, typical of a tertiary halogenoalkane, not a primary one.

OH<sup>−</sup> has lone pairs to donate (Lewis base) and accepts H<sup>+</sup> to form water (Brønsted–Lowry base). BF<sub>3</sub> and [Al(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> are Lewis/BL acids; NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> is a proton donor.

H adds to the C=C carbon with more H atoms (Markovnikov), giving the more stable tertiary carbocation, so Br ends up on C2: 2-bromo-2-methylbutane. 2-bromo-3-methylbutane is the minor product via a secondary carbocation.
A Lewis base donates an electron pair to a Lewis acid, forming a coordination (dative) covalent bond. It is a single shared pair, not a double bond or an intermolecular force.
First nitrate benzene (conc. HNO3/conc. H2SO4) to nitrobenzene, then reduce with Sn/conc. HCl (giving C6H5NH3+), then add NaOH to release phenylamine.
p1.flag: reduction of nitrobenzene not in 2025 guide

p1.key: Hydration (Markovnikov) puts OH on the middle carbon: X = CH3CH(OH)CH3 (propan-2-ol). Hydrogenation with Ni catalyst gives Z = propane. Hydrogenation never forms an alkyne.

A nucleophile donates an electron pair, so it is a Lewis base (I). An electrophile accepts an electron pair, so it is a Lewis acid (II). Lewis acids are by definition electron-pair acceptors (III). All three are correct.
Hex-3-ene, CH3CH2CH=CHCH2CH3, is symmetrical, so adding H2O across the C=C puts OH on C3 either way: hexan-3-ol. "Hexan-4-ol" would be named hexan-3-ol.
Nitrobenzene is reduced by heating with tin and concentrated HCl, giving the phenylammonium ion; NaOH is then added to deprotonate it and release phenylamine.
p1.flag: reduction of nitrobenzene not in 2025 guide

p1.key: A Lewis base donates an electron pair. A nucleophile is an electron-pair donor that attacks electron-deficient centres, so it is a Lewis base. Electrophiles and BF3 are electron-pair acceptors (Lewis acids), and CH4 has no lone pair.
Chlorinating the benzene ring (with a halogen carrier) is electrophilic substitution. Chlorinating the CH3 side chain to CH2Cl happens in UV light, like an alkane, by free-radical substitution.

HCl adds to propene following Markovnikov's rule to give 2-chloropropane (X). NaOH substitutes OH to give propan-2-ol (Y), a secondary alcohol. Excess dichromate oxidizes it to the ketone propanone, CH3COCH3; a secondary alcohol cannot be oxidized to an acid.
A Lewis base must have a lone pair to donate. In NH4+ nitrogen's lone pair is already used in the fourth N–H bond, so it cannot act as a Lewis base. OH−, H2O and PH3 all have lone pairs.
In the ester CH3CH2CH2COO–CH(CH3)2, the acyl part has 4 C (from butanoic acid) and the alkyl part is the isopropyl group, joined through the O of the secondary carbon (from propan-2-ol).

1-Bromopentane (primary) reacts by SN2, while 2-bromo-2-methylbutane (tertiary) reacts by the faster SN1 route via a stable tertiary carbocation, so the primary compound reacts more slowly. C–Br is weaker than C–Cl, so bromopentane reacts faster than chloropentane (C is wrong).

By Markovnikov's rule, H adds to the CH2 end of the double bond and Br to C2 (which gives the more stable secondary carbocation): 2-bromobutane. A single HBr adds only one Br atom, so the dibromo products are impossible.

AlCl3 has an incomplete octet on Al, so it accepts an electron pair (Lewis acid), but it has no H+ to donate, so it is not a Brønsted–Lowry acid. Ethanoic acid and HF are both types of acid, and CCl4 is neither.

By Markovnikov's rule, H adds to the terminal CH2 and Cl to the middle carbon (via the more stable secondary carbocation), giving 2-chloropropane, CH3CHClCH3. Addition removes the double bond, so A and D are impossible.

An aprotic solvent has no H attached to O or N, so it cannot donate H+ or hydrogen-bond as a donor. Methylbenzene (C6H5CH3) has only C–H bonds. Water, methanol and methylamine all have O–H or N–H bonds (protic).
p1.flag: protic/aprotic solvents (S<sub>N</sub>1/S<sub>N</sub>2 context) not explicitly in the 2025 syllabus

p1.key: A nucleophile donates an electron pair to form a new covalent bond, so it must have a lone pair. It need not be negatively charged: neutral H2O and NH3 are nucleophiles.
BF3 has an incomplete octet on boron and accepts an electron pair (Lewis acid), but it has no H+ to donate. H2O can donate protons, and NF3 and NH3 have lone pairs (Lewis bases).

Benzene has a delocalized π system that attracts electrophiles but resists addition, so it reacts with halogens (with a halogen carrier) by electrophilic substitution. Cyclohexane and methylcyclohexane react by free-radical substitution, and cyclohexene by electrophilic addition.
Tertiary halogenoalkanes react fastest by SN1 (stable tertiary carbocation), and the C–I bond is the weakest carbon–halogen bond, making I− the best leaving group. So (CH3)3CI reacts most rapidly.
An electrophile accepts an electron pair, which is the definition of a Lewis acid. Nucleophiles donate electron pairs, so they are Lewis bases.

S<sub>N</sub>1 has two steps via a carbocation intermediate, so the profile has two peaks; the first step (forming the carbocation) is slow, so its peak is higher. Exothermic means products are below reactants.
All three have lone pairs they can donate (Lewis bases), and each can accept a proton (forming HCN, H<sub>2</sub>O and NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>), so all are Brønsted–Lowry bases too.
Propene + HCl → 2-chloropropane (Markovnikov addition); + NaOH → propan-2-ol (substitution); + acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub> → propanone (oxidation of a secondary alcohol).

Cl<sub>2</sub> splits heterolytically (Cl<sup>δ+</sup>/Cl<sup>−</sup>) when it acts as an electrophile: in electrophilic addition to alkenes and in electrophilic substitution of benzene (with a halogen carrier). Nucleophilic substitution does not involve Cl<sub>2</sub>.
I: Br replaced by OH (nucleophilic substitution); II: primary alcohol → carboxylic acid (oxidation); III: carboxylic acid → aldehyde (reduction).
The nitronium ion NO2+ is an electrophile that replaces an H on the ring; the aromatic ring is kept, so the mechanism is electrophilic substitution, not addition.
